pedagogy.summary: Year 4 (age 8–9) draws the measures strands together: pupils ESTIMATE, COMPARE and CALCULATE across different measures — length, mass, capacity and money in pounds and pence. Three distinct skills sit here. Estimation means producing a reasoned rough value (and using it to sense-check exact work). Comparison across units requires converting to a common unit first (1.5 kg vs 1200 g → 1500 g > 1200 g). Calculation with money now uses decimal £.p as one quantity. The recurring hazard across all three is treating a measure as two separate whole numbers (2 m 30 cm, £3.47) or comparing raw digits while ignoring units.
bestPractices: Teach estimation as a deliberate step BEFORE exact calculation — round each price/measure to something friendly (£2.45 ≈ £2, 1.30 ≈ £1), get an approximate total, then compute exactly and CHECK the exact answer against the estimate.
For comparison, always convert to a common unit first and make the conversion explicit (1.5 kg = 1500 g); use double number lines or a bar to show why the digits alone can't be compared.
Use benchmarks/referents for estimation (a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1-litre bottle, a £1 coin) so estimates are anchored, not guessed.
Handle money totals as single decimal quantities, aligning by the decimal point and exchanging 100p→£1; connect £.p place value to metric decimals (2.30 m, £2.30).
Make 'is this answer reasonable?' a routine — an unreasonable exact answer signals an error to find.
keyRepresentations: Benchmark referents (metre stick, 1 kg mass, 1 litre, £1 coin) for anchoring estimates
Double number line / bar model for comparing across units
Place-value columns aligned by the decimal point (metric measures and money)
Rounding number line for estimation before exact calculation
commonMisconceptions: Compares across units by digits alone, ignoring the unit ('1200 g > 1.5 kg because 1200 > 1.5').
Skips estimation and so cannot judge whether an exact answer is reasonable.
'String-length thinking' persists in totals — treats £2.45 or 2 m 30 cm as two separate whole numbers when adding.
Rounds after calculating rather than before, or rounds the wrong way, so the estimate is useless as a check.

learn.summary: Year 4 (age 8–9) learners estimate, compare and calculate across measures — length, mass, capacity and money in pounds and pence. Three distinct skills sit together: estimation (producing a reasoned rough value and using it to sense-check exact work), comparison across units (converting to a common unit first, e.g. 1.5 kg = 1500 g > 1200 g), and calculation with money as a single decimal £.p quantity. The recurring hazard across all three is treating a measure as two separate whole numbers (2 m 30 cm, £3.47) or comparing raw digits while ignoring units.

activities.title: Measure bench: estimate first, then check
feedback: If the learner skips the estimate and goes straight to an exact total: ask 'Before you worked it out exactly, what did you EXPECT the answer to be about — and does your exact answer match that?' Build the habit of rounding and adding for a ballpark first.

If an out-of-range exact answer is accepted without comment (e.g. £45 or £0.45 for the three items): point back to the estimate of about £4 and ask whether the result is plausible, then help locate the error.
If rounding happens after calculating or the wrong way, so the estimate cannot act as a check: practise rounding each amount before computing and comparing the two.
activities.rationale: Research cited here (NCETM, unverified in this row) suggests learners often skip estimating before calculating and so may lack a sense of a sensible answer, leaving errors undetected; committing the estimate before the exact value is revealed is intended to make reasonableness-checking a routine. A live estimate→reveal→gap loop (committing an estimate, then revealing the exact value and showing the error) is a proposed way to make the check concrete, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Pupils rarely estimate before calculating and so lack a sense of a sensible answer, leaving errors undetected.
learnerActions: Face a task: three priced items (£2.45, £1.30, £0.75) to total, or two measures to compare.

Round each amount to something friendly (£2.45≈£2, £1.30≈£1, £0.75≈£1) and commit a rough estimate BEFORE seeing any exact answer — for example drag a slider or write the estimate down and lock it in.
Keep benchmark referents in view while estimating (a £1 coin, a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1-litre bottle) so the estimate is anchored rather than guessed.
Only after the estimate is committed, reveal/compute the exact total (£4.50) and look at the gap between estimate and truth.
Decide out loud whether the exact answer is reasonable: does it land near the estimate (about £4)? If not, treat that as a flag to find an error.
activities.intendedInsight: An exact answer that lands far from a sensible estimate signals a likely error; landing near it makes the answer plausible, though it cannot catch every small slip (e.g. £4.40 instead of £4.50). Estimation is a deliberate step before calculation and a checkable habit afterwards, not an afterthought.

activities.title: Convert before you compare: the balance that tips
feedback: If the learner picks the larger NUMBER regardless of unit ('1200 g is heavier because 1200 > 1.5'): ask 'What is 1.5 kg in grams? Now which is more?' and make converting to a common unit the first step every time.
Offer the counterexample 'What if the bag were 1.5 kg and the other were 1500 g — which is heavier then?' to show they are equal once converted.
If conversion is shaky, rehearse on a double number line or balance that you can only compare like with like.
activities.rationale: Comparison across units requires converting to a common unit first; making the conversion explicit (and, optionally, physically felt on a balance or number line) targets the digits-only misconception. A 3D balance or filling a container can add physicality to mass/capacity work, though the core reasoning is numeric rather than inherently spatial.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should estimate, compare and calculate different measures, including money in pounds and pence; non-statutory guidance says they build on place value and decimal notation to record metric measures including money, and use multiplication to convert from larger to smaller units.
learnerActions: Take two measures in different units, e.g. 1.5 kg and 1200 g.
Before deciding which is larger, convert both to a common unit: 1.5 kg = 1500 g (using multiplication by 1000 from larger to smaller unit), or convert 1200 g = 1.2 kg.
Compare only once the units match: 1500 g > 1200 g, so 1.5 kg is heavier.

Optionally use a double number line or bar model to show why the raw digits (1.5 vs 1200) cannot be compared directly; a balance-scale tool that rewrites 1.5 kg as 1500 g and tips against 1200 g lets the comparison be seen rather than asserted.
Order a short set across units, e.g. 1.5 kg / 1200 g / 900 g, after converting all to grams (1500 g, 1200 g, 900 g).
activities.intendedInsight: To compare two measures reliably, first express them in the same unit; comparing the raw digits while ignoring the units can give the wrong answer (1200 > 1.5, yet 1200 g < 1.5 kg).

activities.title: Money as one quantity: totalling £.p
feedback: If the total has three digits after the point, or pounds and pence are added independently, or amounts are not lined up by the decimal point: return to £.p as one quantity, realign by the decimal point and exchange 100p for £1.
Connect back to metric decimals (2.30 m) so the same place-value reasoning transfers across measures.
Self-check the three items: pence 45+30+75 = 150p = £1.50, pounds 2+1+0 = £3, giving £4.50 — use this to confirm the total.
activities.rationale: The 'two separate whole numbers' error affects measurement as well as money (using '2 m and 30 cm' as two whole numbers instead of 230 cm), driven by whole-number language; competence with two-place money amounts does not guarantee wider decimal understanding, so handling money as a single aligned decimal quantity is deliberately taught.
sourceClaims: The 'two separate whole numbers' error affects measurement as well as money — e.g. using '2 m and 30 cm' as two whole numbers instead of 230 cm — driven by whole-number language; competence with two-place money amounts does not guarantee wider decimal understanding.
learnerActions: Total three amounts such as £2.45, £1.30 and £0.75.
Treat each amount as a single decimal quantity, not as two separate whole numbers; align the amounts by the decimal point.
Add, exchanging 100p for £1 where the pence exceed 99, to get £4.50.
Check the result reads place-value-honestly: two digits after the point, not three (£3.150 would signal pence added past 100 without exchanging).
Connect £.p place value to metric decimals written the same way, e.g. 2.30 m alongside £2.30.
activities.intendedInsight: Money totals are single decimal quantities: aligning by the decimal point and exchanging 100p→£1 avoids 'string-length thinking' that adds pounds and pence as independent whole-number columns.

activities.title: Benchmark estimation across length, mass and capacity
feedback: Ask 'Estimate the length of this classroom in metres. What did you use to help you decide — a metre stick? a stride?' to surface whether the estimate is anchored.
If an estimate seems arbitrary, point to a concrete referent (metre stick, 1 kg bag, 1-litre bottle, £1 coin) and re-anchor.
Prompt transfer: having estimated a length, ask the learner to use the same rounding-then-check move on a money total or a mass.
activities.rationale: The DfE programme of study expects pupils to estimate across different measures and to transfer the routine between measure types; anchoring estimates to physical benchmarks/referents is a pedagogy-level recommendation (from the row's best practice) rather than a directly cited finding, so it is offered as a reasoned proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should estimate, compare and calculate different measures, including money in pounds and pence; non-statutory guidance says they build on place value and decimal notation to record metric measures including money, and use multiplication to convert from larger to smaller units.
learnerActions: Estimate the length of the classroom in metres before measuring, stating what referent you used (a metre stick, a stride).
Estimate a mass against a known 1 kg bag, or a capacity against a 1-litre bottle.
Say the estimate aloud and the reasoning behind it, then measure or compute the exact value and compare.
Transfer the estimate→convert→calculate routine across length, mass, capacity and money rather than only within one measure type.
activities.intendedInsight: Good estimates come from anchoring to physical benchmarks you know, and the same estimate-then-check routine works across every measure.

constraints: Estimation must be committed BEFORE the exact value is revealed or calculated — otherwise it cannot serve as a check and becomes an afterthought.

A labelled picture or benchmark image can show what a metre, 1 kg or £1 looks like, but on its own cannot run the estimate-then-check loop or a unit conversion; use it as a referent, not as the full activity.

Recognition/ordering formats (choose-the-heavier, order these) can rehearse and check each skill crisply but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own free reasoning; pair them with prompts asking the learner to state and justify the estimate and the conversion.

A 3D balance or container adds physicality to mass/capacity comparison but is optional; the core reasoning (convert, compare, estimate) is numeric and not inherently spatial, and is not needed for money or estimation.

Interaction examples (slider to commit an estimate, a balance that rewrites 1.5 kg as 1500 g and tips, double number lines, decimal-aligned place-value columns) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory tools.

Role-play dialogue does not by itself require the learner to carry out the estimation or unit conversion this objective targets, so on its own it may not elicit the procedural steps; if used, direct it to prompt the learner to state and justify an estimate rather than relying on it to teach the procedure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic self-check: £2.45 + £1.30 + £0.75 = £4.50 (pence 45+30+75 = 150p = £1.50; pounds 2+1+0 = £3). This confirms the stated exact total.
Unit check: 1.5 kg = 1500 g > 1200 g, so 1.5 kg is correctly the heavier mass; the digits-only reading (1.5 < 1200) is the misconception, not a valid comparison.

One source (NCETM, 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives') is marked verified:false in the row; its claim about learners rarely estimating is retained but treated as unverified, and the rationale wording was softened accordingly. Treating estimation-before-calculation as a habit is pedagogically reasonable but its efficacy is not independently established here.
Benchmark anchoring of estimates is drawn from the row's best-practice/pedagogy notes rather than from a directly cited source claim; it is retained as a reasoned recommendation.

The original framing that a live 2D interaction is 'exactly' the ideal and static/dialogue formats are 'poor' reflects a catalog preference, not established comparative efficacy; retained as design suggestions with stated affordances/limits rather than universal laws.

probeDeeper: 'Before you worked it out exactly, what did you EXPECT the answer to be about — and does your exact answer match that?'
'You said 1200 g is heavier — what is 1.5 kg in grams? Now which is more?'
'What if the bag were 1.5 kg and the other were 1500 g — which is heavier then?' (counterexample: equal once converted).
'Estimate the length of this classroom in metres. What did you use to help you decide — a metre stick? a stride?'
assess.correctAnswer: Gives a reasoned estimate first (≈£2 + £1 + £1 = £4, or 'about £4.50') THEN the exact £4.50, and uses the estimate to check it. For the masses: 1.5 kg is heavier because 1.5 kg = 1500 g, which is more than 1200 g — stated by converting to a common unit, not by comparing 1.5 with 1200.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares across units by the digits, ignoring the unit — 'the 1200 g is heavier because 1200 is bigger than 1.5' (or bigger than 15).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make units common first, every time: convert 1.5 kg → 1500 g (or 1200 g → 1.2 kg) on a double number line or balance, then compare; rehearse that you can only compare like with like.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the item with the larger NUMBER regardless of unit; does not convert 1.5 kg to 1500 g before deciding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Skips estimation and cannot judge reasonableness — goes straight to an exact calculation, produces an unreasonable total (e.g. £45 or £0.45 for the three items) and doesn't notice it's wrong.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place: build the habit of rounding each amount and adding for a ballpark BEFORE calculating, then checking the exact answer against it — an exact answer far from the estimate flags an error to find.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No rough answer offered before calculating; an out-of-range exact answer accepted without comment.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'String-length thinking' in the money total — treats £2.45, £1.30, £0.75 as separate whole-number columns, adding pence past 100 without exchanging (e.g. £3.150) or misaligning the decimal points.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to £.p as one quantity: align by the decimal point, exchange 100p for £1, and read the total place-value-honestly; connect to metric decimals (2.30 m).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A total with three digits after the point, or pounds and pence added independently, or amounts not lined up by the decimal point.

responseLevels.gap: Compares raw numbers ignoring units, offers no estimate, and cannot total £.p reliably; accepts unreasonable answers.
responseLevels.full: Estimates before calculating and uses the estimate to check; converts to a common unit before comparing; totals money as a single quantity; and transfers the estimate–convert–calculate routine across length, mass, capacity and money.
responseLevels.partial: Calculates exactly and/or converts for a friendly case, but does not estimate to check, or can compare only when the units already match — lists results without judging reasonableness or transferring across measure types.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put three price tags in front of the child — £2.45, £1.30, £0.75 — and say: 'First tell me ROUGHLY what these cost altogether, then work out the exact total.' Then show a 1.5 kg bag and a 1200 g bag and ask: 'Which is heavier — and how do you know?' Watch whether they estimate before calculating, and whether they convert before comparing.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the idea estimates first (rounding sensibly) and converts to a common unit before comparing, so 1.5 kg is correctly heavier; a child who lacks it dives straight to an exact calculation with no reasonableness check, and/or judges 1200 g heavier because 1200 > 1.5 (or > 15). Estimating-before and converting-before each produce a visibly different move from the wrong ideas.
